sources.title: Serbia Election Marks the End of an Era | Council on Foreign Relations
sources.text: Council on Foreign Relations Articles Share By experts and staff Published October 27, 2026  10:20 p.m. Charles A. Kupchan CFR Expert Senior Fellow Ivana Saric CFR Editor Share Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led opposition movement in Serbia’s October 25 parliamentary elections, ending his party’s fourteen years in power. Vucic had called snap elections in a bid to regain his previous post as prime minister, but the list led by his populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) managed just under 40 percent of the vote compared with around 53 percent for the opposition Student List. Pollsters and the Republic Electoral Commission estimated turnout at nearly 70 percent, which Reuters noted was the highest turnout since the breakup of Yugoslavia. The vote came after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the deaths of sixteen people when a canopy collapsed at a renovated railway station in Novi Sad, a disaster that protesters blamed on corruption and cronyism . Some opposition parliamentary parties supported the student movement, which demanded early elections. It put forth a list of 250 candidates—including doctors, professors, farmers, and activists. Most opposition parties declined to field their own candidates and urged supporters to back the Student List. Several ran anyway, although no non-minority list outside the Student List and the SNS-led coalition crossed the 3 percent threshold. Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) and author of the new book Bringing Order to Anarchy: Governing the World to Come , spoke with CFR about the election results—and what they might mean—following his recent trip to Belgrade. You just returned from Belgrade. What was the mood like on the ground? I arrived last Thursday evening. In the city center, where my hotel was located, a massive protest was taking place; the crowd was estimated at around 150,000 people. The atmosphere was electric. The crowd was singing and chanting as it coursed through the streets, excited by the prospect that the Vucic era was about to come to an end. There were police everywhere and lots of streets cordoned off, but I saw no confrontations or violence. In my conversations on Friday and Saturday—I was at the University of Belgrade—students and faculty expressed cautious optimism that the Student List would prevail. In the end, a very high turnout helped the opposition win. Based on your conversations there, what were the main drivers of dissatisfaction with Vucic’s party? The student movement reflected a spontaneous mobilization of civil society that spread broadly across the country. One of the main slogans of this movement was “Serbia or the mafia,” indicating exasperation with years of corruption and state capture. The student movement now has wind in its sails and lots of political momentum. It needs to focus on turning that momentum into good policies and good governance. What does Vucic’s defeat mean for Serbia and its relationships with the European Union (EU), Russia, and its Balkan neighbors? It is difficult to say, because the Student List opposition campaigned mainly on domestic issues. Once a new government forms, it is likely to focus on fighting corruption, purging Vucic loyalists from the ministries and public enterprises, opening up a media community that had been dominated by Vucic, implementing economic reforms, and reducing political patronage. Relations with the EU are likely to improve as democratic reforms move forward. Ties to Russia may well grow more distant. Although it is unclear if the new government will try to move forward on relations with Kosovo, the change of government opens up the possibility of rekindling the normalization dialogue between Belgrade and Pristina. What challenges are ahead for the movement as it shifts to the task of governing? There is no clear leader of the Student List, and, as you noted, many of the winning candidates have little or no political experience. So the key challenge will be moving from a grassroots movement that inspired many voters across Serbia to governing a country that has long been run by Vucic and his embedded network of supporters. The movement has its work cut out. This work represents the views solely of the author(s). In short: President Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in Serbia's parliamentary elections. Mr Vučić called a snap election in September after almost two years of student-led protests. What's next? Polls showed the students' candidate list would have 138 deputies, while Mr Vučić's SNS party garnered 104 seats in the 250-seat parliament. abc.net.au/news/serbia-election-vucic-defeat-student-protest/107307808 Link copied Share Share article Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić has conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement in parliamentary elections. "We still do not have final results [but] on the basis of a sample … it is clear that we have lost these elections," Mr Vučić said on Sunday. "The Student List has won. They will have between 135 and 140 seats, and we will have 105. Aleksandar Vučić ruled Serbia for 14 years. ( Reuters: Zorana Jevtic ) "No-one else has entered parliament." Mr Vučić called the snap elections in September, after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism. The protests were initially triggered by a train station canopy collapse in the city of Novi Sad in 2024 that killed 16 people. The election results follow almost two years of student-led protests against the government. ( Reuters: Marko Djurica ) Belgrade's streets erupted in celebration after Mr Vučić's announcement, with cars honking and students shouting "victory" and "he's done". "Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, said, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. " Tonight we celebrate victory. Tomorrow we build the future. " People took to the streets of Belgrade to celebrate. ( Reuters: Zorana Jevtic ) Mr Vučić, endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and denouncing the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led the Balkan country for 14 years. Turnout was nearly 70 per cent, the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992. Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia on Sunday, signalling a widespread desire for change. A large percentage of Serbians turned up to vote in this election. ( Reuters: Marko Djurica ) "For decades the people have been waiting for this time, something to bring hope that we can live freely and by the rules of democracy," said actor Jelena Stupljanin, 48, at a Belgrade polling station. Uncertainty over students' candidates A representative sample by the CESID-IPSPS pollsters showed the student's candidate list would have 138 deputies, while Mr Vučić's SNS party garnered 104 seats in the 250-seat parliament. The remaining seats will be shared between ethnic national minority parties. Much remains unclear about how the student-backed candidates will fare. Their list of 250 largely unknown personalities includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although it is still unclear who will be prime minister. People celebrate the student movement's electoral victory. ( Reuters: Marko Djurica ) The students' domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling. Political analysts predict some kind of purge of Vučić allies in the police, security services and ministries. The students have been quieter about their international ambitions, but they will have to balance relations with China, a major investor; Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and main supplier of natural gas; and the European Union, Serbia's largest trading partner.
